title: Gerrit webhook Cloud Function is public and accepts forged events without any authentication, enabling attacker-chosen staging deploys
description: The gerrit-webhook Cloud Function is granted roles/run.invoker to allUsers, justified by a comment claiming Gerrit verifies calls via HMAC. The handler never verifies any signature, secret, OIDC token or source IP. It dispatches purely on the body-supplied 'type'. A forged change-merged event with branch master and an arbitrary newRev makes the function record that SHA as staging's targetSha and enqueue a staging deploy of it. The builder agent then fetches and hard-resets to that ref and deploys it to staging, bypassing Gerrit review/submit. Forged patchset-created, nightly-* and reconcile-verifies events can also trigger builder work.
root_cause: Authentication was delegated to a non-existent application-layer HMAC check: the Cloud Run service is opened to allUsers and Handle() trusts the unauthenticated JSON body, including type, Change.Branch and NewRev.
intended_behavior: Only Gerrit (webhook with shared-secret HMAC or authenticated invoker) and Cloud Scheduler (OIDC) should be able to invoke the function; event content should be accepted only from an authenticated sender.

trace.description: Public HTTP handler reads the raw body and unmarshals it with no signature, secret, token or IP check, then switches on attacker-controlled event.Type.
Trusts event.Change.Branch (only must equal master) and event.NewRev as the merged commit; no verification against Gerrit that the SHA was merged.
Writes attacker-supplied SHA as staging targetSha and into pending changelog in Firestore, which also marks legitimate pending deploys as superseded.

Cancels queued auto-deploys and enqueues a staging deploy Task with Ref set to the forged SHA; the agent (agent/main.go:669 git.Checkout, agent/actions/git/checkout.go:60 fetch and :95 reset --hard FETCH_HEAD) fetches that ref with the bot credential and deploys it to staging.

evidence.description: google_cloud_run_v2_service_iam_member gerrit_webhook_invoker grants roles/run.invoker to allUsers (line 69); preceding comment at line 63 claims HMAC verification that does not exist in code.
Handle has no authentication; grep of the gerrit module finds no hmac/signature/X-Gerrit/oidc verification anywhere in the function path.
Scheduler jobs call the function URL with plain POST and no oidc_token, confirming the function is intended to be callable unauthenticated.
RecordMerge and CreateDeploy (line 358) are called with event.NewRev taken directly from the request body.

tryAutoSubmit relies on Gerrit ChangeSubmittable/ChangeMergeable checks, so forged comment-added cannot force-submit unapproved changes; impact there is limited to triggering legitimate submits early.

conditions.description: None required to call the function; attacker needs only the function URL (not secret, deterministic cloudfunctions/run.app URL).

For arbitrary code to reach staging the attacker needs a SHA fetchable from code.nile.ag by the bot (e.g. a pushed unreviewed refs/changes patchset, which requires a Gerrit account, or any existing unmerged/merged SHA). Without a Gerrit account the attacker can only replay existing commits, supersede/disrupt legitimate staging deploys, and spam builder tasks.

Only staging is auto-targeted by this path; production deploys are manually requested and not reachable via this event. Cloud Run ingress is not restricted in the Terraform (no ingress setting found).

execution.attacker_perspective: Anonymous internet caller who knows the webhook function URL.
instructions: Send the POST with Content-Type application/json to the public function URL.
Handler records the SHA as staging targetSha and enqueues a staging deploy; the builder fetches and deploys it.
execution.observed_result: Source-level observation, not a runtime result: no check exists on any path between the allUsers invoker binding and the deploy enqueue, so the forged event is accepted and acted upon.

remediation.strategy: Remove allUsers invoker. Require authentication: configure Gerrit webhook with a shared secret and verify the HMAC (constant-time) over the raw body in Handle before parsing, and give Cloud Scheduler an oidc_token with an invoker-only service account. Additionally, in handleChangeMerged confirm via the Gerrit API that NewRev is the merged tip of master for the given change before recording/deploying.

likelihood.reason: Fully unauthenticated and trivial to send, but requires knowing the function URL and, for attacker code, a Gerrit account to produce a fetchable unreviewed SHA; Gerrit fetch-by-SHA policy is not visible in source.

impact.reason: Bypasses review to deploy an attacker-chosen commit to staging and disrupts the deploy pipeline; production not directly reachable, so blast radius limited to staging and builder resources.

confidence.reason: Absence of auth is directly visible in the handler, terraform IAM binding and scheduler config; the only uncertainty is deployment facts limiting which SHAs the agent can fetch.

title: Zip-slip in harvester Potatoes SA archive extraction (no containment of entry names)
description: The harvester downloads a zip from a URL returned by the third-party api.potatoes.co.za endpoint and extracts every entry using the attacker-controlled entry name in the destination path with no containment check. The path arithmetic does not neutralise traversal. The entry name is prefixed with 'YYMMDD_', which becomes one extra path segment. path.Join then lexically cleans 'tmp/260101_/../../x' to '<parent of tmp>/x', so the prefix consumes one '..' and a second '..' escapes os.TempDir(). Entries with three or more '..' go further up. Absolute entry names stay under the temp dir because of the prefix. Go's archive/zip accepts '..' names by default; no GODEBUG zipinsecurepath setting was found in the repo. The result is an arbitrary file create/truncate and write as the harvester process user, with contents controlled by the zip provider. The directory branch (os.MkdirAll on a relative, prefixed name) is a lesser variant. The source path is fully established. Exploitability depends on the provider being malicious or compromised, on the process user and filesystem permissions in the harvester container, and on what is writable and later consumed. These are deployment facts, so the verdict is needs_validation and not confirmed.
claimed_root_cause: unzipFile builds the output path with path.Join(os.TempDir(), date+'_'+f.Name) and calls os.Create and io.Copy without checking that the cleaned path remains inside the intended extraction directory. The date prefix does not prevent escape, because a single prefix segment is cancelled by one '..' during path.Clean.

trace.description: The JSON body from the third-party https://api.potatoes.co.za/external/nile/<date> endpoint (authenticated with a Bearer token) is decoded, and ex.URL is returned unvalidated. This is the lower-trust external data feed.
The provider-supplied URL is fetched with no host or scheme check. The body is written to os.TempDir()/<date>_potatoes_sa.zip (lines 88-94), so the provider controls the full zip contents.
zip.OpenReader opens the archive; f.Name for each entry is attacker-controlled. Go's default behaviour does not reject '..' names (the zipinsecurepath GODEBUG setting is not set in the repo).
fp = path.Join(os.TempDir(), 'YYMMDD_' + f.Name). The name '../../x' cleans to '<parent of tmp>/x', escaping the temp dir. There is no prefix or containment check.
os.Create(fp) creates or truncates the file at the escaped path, and io.Copy (line 132) writes the entry contents into it. The sink is an arbitrary file write as the harvester user.

evidence.description: fileDelimiter is '_' and dateFormat is '060102' (line 8). The prefix is therefore the single segment 'YYMMDD_', which one '..' cancels, so it does not block traversal.
newFileName concatenates the date, the delimiter and the raw entry name with no sanitisation.
The directory branch calls os.MkdirAll on the prefixed relative name, with no containment and no temp-dir anchoring.
unzipFile is called directly on the downloaded archive, with no intermediate validation of entry names.
The toolchain is Go 1.27. The repo has no zipinsecurepath GODEBUG setting, so '..' entry names are accepted by archive/zip.
The runtime image is docker.io/chromedp/headless-shell:stable. No USER directive was seen in the grep, so the container user and filesystem writability are unresolved from source.

blockers: The provider (api.potatoes.co.za) is a contracted partner feed. Whether it is a realistic lower-trust principal, or could be compromised or tampered with in transit, is a threat-model fact not in source.

The harvester container runtime user, read-only root filesystem setting and writable mounts are not in source (the Dockerfile has no USER directive). These determine what an escaped write can overwrite and what impact follows.
The runtime Go behaviour (GODEBUG zipinsecurepath) in the deployed binary was not observed, and no code could be run in this review.

validation_plan.local: In a throwaway Go test or sandbox with a scratch directory and no network, build a zip containing an entry named '../../probe.txt' and call unzipFile on it with TMPDIR set to a nested scratch subdirectory. Confirm whether the file appears outside that TMPDIR. Also confirm that zip.OpenReader does not return ErrInsecurePath under the repo's Go 1.27 and GODEBUG defaults.
validation_plan.deployment: Owner to inspect the harvester Cloud Run or container configuration for the runtime UID, read-only root filesystem and writable mounts (inspect only, no live probing). Also confirm the contractual and TLS trust relationship with the Potatoes SA API and whether the endpoint or token has ever been exposed. If the container runs non-root with a read-only filesystem, downgrade to low or informational. Regardless, fix by rejecting entries whose cleaned path is not inside a dedicated extraction directory, using filepath.IsLocal or filepath.Rel, and by extracting into os.MkdirTemp instead of the shared temp dir.

title: nilocloud Gerrit Checks endpoints (/v1/gerrit/checks, /checks/log, /checks/run) have no authentication
description: Source-level: the three Gerrit Checks routes are wrapped only by gerritCorsMiddleware, which just sets CORS headers (and CORS is not an access control for non-browser callers). Every other sensitive route in the same mux uses authMiddleware (robot token). The nilocloud Cloud Run service is deployed with --allow-unauthenticated. An unauthenticated caller can therefore (a) POST /v1/gerrit/checks/run?change=N&patchset=M to enqueue a verify Cloud Task, which first deletes queued verify tasks whose names start with change-N-ps-, marks pending runs for that change stale in Firestore, then enqueues a new task and rewrites GCS state with a bumped attempt number; (b) GET the per-patchset checks state JSON; (c) GET check logs by externalId. Impact is bounded by source: the ref is always built server-side by RefForChange as refs/changes/NN/N/M from validated positive ints, the task is the same verify that webhook.go:169 and reconcile.go:121 already trigger for every uploaded patchset, and ValidExternalID restricts the log id to the anchored regex ^\d+-\d+-\d+-(known check name)$, so there is no path traversal in LogPath. The verify task runs checks (codegen, lint, test) on whatever the Gerrit change contains, but anyone able to upload a change already gets that automatically, so forged verifies do not create new code-execution reach for an outsider. Real effects are limited to unauthenticated CI cost and queue abuse, cancel-and-replace of legitimate queued verifies and attempt counter churn (integrity and availability of CI status), and disclosure of CI state and log content. Whether this is a meaningful boundary violation depends on facts not in source: network exposure of the service (Cloud Run ingress, any fronting proxy or IAP), whether the checks bucket logs contain sensitive output, and whether the Gerrit instance itself is internet reachable.
claimed_root_cause: Gerrit checks routes were registered without authMiddleware or any other identity or authorization check, and rely on CORS (Allow-Origin https://code.nile.ag) as if it were access control, on a service deployed with --allow-unauthenticated.

trace.description: Routes /v1/gerrit/checks, /checks/log, /checks/run (lines 26-28) are registered with gerritCorsMiddleware only; no authMiddleware, unlike the webhook, events and subscription routes above them.
Only sets Access-Control-* headers and short-circuits OPTIONS; performs no authentication or origin enforcement on the actual request.
Requires POST and positive integer change and patchset query params (lines 85-103), then calls task.CreateVerify at line 115 without any caller identity check.

deleteQueuedTasks removes queued verify tasks for the change (line 64), a new Cloud Task is enqueued, queued runs are superseded in Firestore (line 83), and initial SCHEDULED state is written to GCS (line 93). Ref is built by RefForChange from integers only.
Reads and returns GCS log object for an id that passes the anchored ValidExternalID regex (line 137); the checks state handler similarly reads state at line 48. Both return data to any caller.

evidence.description: Contrast: sentry/grafana webhooks and subscriptions are wrapped in authMiddleware; the Gerrit checks routes at lines 26-28 are not.
nilocloud is deployed to Cloud Run with --allow-unauthenticated (deployment config as written; live IAM and ingress not verified).
externalIDRe is anchored and limited to digits plus a known check-name alternation, so log reads cannot traverse paths.
RefForChange builds the ref from integers only, so an attacker cannot select an arbitrary ref or repo.
The same CreateVerify is invoked automatically for every uploaded patchset, so the forged trigger adds no new code-execution capability for outsiders.

blockers: Cloud Run ingress and IAM for nilocloud (and any fronting proxy or IAP) are not visible in source; --allow-unauthenticated in cloudbuild.yaml may be overridden or the service may sit behind an internal-only network.
Sensitivity of content in the GCS checks bucket (state JSON and full check output logs) is unknown; it may include source snippets or env-derived output.
Cloud Tasks queue and agent concurrency or cost limits that bound the abuse impact are not in source.

validation_plan.deployment: Owner check, read-only: run gcloud run services describe nilocloud --region europe-west4 and inspect ingress annotation and the IAM policy for allUsers roles/run.invoker; confirm whether code.nile.ag or the service URL is reachable from outside the corporate network. Review a sample of objects in the checks bucket for sensitive content. Do not probe the live service with forged requests against real changes.
validation_plan.local: Source-only: confirm via a unit test using httptest against Resolver.ServeHTTP with a stubbed task client that an unauthenticated POST to /v1/gerrit/checks/run reaches CreateVerify; then decide on a fix such as requiring a Gerrit-issued or shared-secret token, a Google ID token check, or restricting ingress.

title: Horus /horus Slack command and unblock action have no operator allowlist or approval step beyond the Slack signature
description: The /horus slash-command endpoint and the Slack interactive-actions endpoint authenticate only that the request was signed by Slack (SLACK_SIGNING_SECRET). Nothing in nilocloud or the gerrit task layer checks who invoked the command. user_name is read from the form and used only as a display or attribution string. Any Slack workspace member who can invoke /horus can enqueue production deploys, production DB migrations (including direction down), Play Store Android builds, and market image builds. Any member who can click the Grafana unblock button can unblock a consumer; the interaction user in the callback is never consulted. Source shows no per-user, per-channel, per-team or approval gate on any path. Whether this is a real violation depends on the intended authority of Slack workspace members and on Slack-side command or channel restrictions, which are deployment facts outside source.
claimed_root_cause: Authorization for privileged CI/CD operations is delegated entirely to Slack workspace membership. After verifySlack, HandleSlack dispatches on the text field with no identity-based authorization (no user_id, channel_id or team_id check), and task.CreateDeploy, CreateMigrate, CreateBuildMarket and CreateAndroidBuild enqueue Cloud Tasks without any actor check. handleSlackActions ignores cb.User and the channel.

trace.description: Slash-command endpoint reachable by Slack. A request is accepted if it carries a valid Slack signature.
Only control is the HMAC signing-secret check. The form is parsed and passed to horus.HandleSlack at line 78. No user or channel allowlist.
Reads text and user_name (lines 48-49) and dispatches on parts[0] with no identity check. user_name is passed as an attribution string only.

Accepts env=production from arbitrary args, validated only against a service-name list. Calls task.CreateDeploy, CreateMigrate (direction up or down), CreateBuildMarket and CreateAndroidBuild directly.

trace.scope: CreateMigrate (CreateDeploy at gerrit/task/deploy.go:107 is the sibling)
trace.description: Validates only the service name, then enqueues a Cloud Task (createTask) that runs the migration or deploy against the chosen environment. actor/triggerName is only recorded as TriggerName. No authorization or approval.

Signed interaction callback. For ActionIDUnblockConsumer it calls GrafanaResolver().UnblockConsumer (line 121) using service, consumer id and cursor from the button value. cb.User and the channel are never checked.

evidence.description: Signature verification uses SLACK_SIGNING_SECRET (key name only). It is the sole authentication on the horus, actions and events handlers.

deploy, build, migrate, test and verify handlers all receive only userName for attribution. No allowlist, role or approval logic exists anywhere in the horus package (grep for allow, authori, user_id, channel_id, team_id, approv returned nothing).
Production and down are accepted as plain args for migrate, with no extra confirmation.
The actor is stored only as TriggerName. The task layer has no authorization.
The Horus section describes only the Slack bot and mise CLI parity. It states no authorization model, so the intended operator authority is undocumented in source.

blockers: Intended authority of Slack workspace members is a design fact outside source. If /horus is meant to be usable by all members of a private, trusted engineering workspace or channel, this is accepted design, not a violation.
Slack app configuration is not in source. The slash command's availability (restricted channels or user groups, workspace guest/external-member policy, Slack Connect) is unknown.
Downstream enforcement is not in source. The worker may require Gerrit/IAM-level or environment-level protections for production, and Cloud Run ingress or IAM for the endpoint is unknown.

(1) In the Slack app admin console, list who can use /horus: which workspaces and channels, whether guests, restricted accounts or Slack Connect members are in them, and whether the command is limited via Slack app permissions or workflow restrictions. (2) Confirm with the platform owners whether any workspace member is intended to be able to queue production deploys and migrate down. (3) Check the Cloud Run IAM and ingress settings on nilocloud and the Cloud Tasks consumer's production guards in the infra config. Do not send live probes or trigger production tasks.

A further local check could run unit tests against HandleSlack with a stub task layer, but this is unnecessary because the absence of a check is already visible in source.

title: nilocloud: one NILO_ROBOT_TOKEN gates both inbound Sentry/Grafana webhooks (token in URL query) and the browser-callable consumer-unblock action
description: authMiddleware in nilocloud uses a single env secret, NILO_ROBOT_TOKEN, for two different purposes. For /v1/webhooks/* it is read from the query string (?robotToken=), so it sits in webhook URLs configured in third-party tools (Sentry, Grafana) and potentially in request logs. For /v1/events/unblock it is read from 'Authorization: Bearer robotToken=<token>', and the endpoint is called directly from a browser (Grafana table action, CORS allow-origin https://obs.nile.ag). A successful call publishes a consumer-unblock Pub/Sub job. The job handler then advances the named consumer's cursor, which permanently skips the event at expected_cursor+1, and posts a Slack notice. Any holder of the webhook URL (Sentry/Grafana config readers, log readers) therefore also holds authority to skip events in ledger, trader, administrator and other consumers. Source review shows no per-purpose credential separation and a non-constant-time compare. TrimPrefix also means a bare token without the 'Bearer robotToken=' prefix is accepted. Whether this crosses a real trust boundary depends on who can read the Sentry/Grafana webhook configuration, the Grafana action config, and the Cloud Run request logs. Those are deployment facts not visible in source. Same-principal ops staff holding both capabilities would not be a finding. Hardening-grade unless the token is shown to leak to a lower-trust party.
claimed_root_cause: A single shared static secret (NILO_ROBOT_TOKEN) authorizes both low-privilege inbound webhook delivery (credential carried in a URL query string) and a state-changing operational action (consumer unblock/skip), with no scoping, rotation separation or constant-time comparison.

trace.description: Route /v1/events/unblock (all methods, so OPTIONS preflight works) wrapped in grafanaCorsMiddleware(authMiddleware(unblockConsumerHandler)); reachable from a browser on obs.nile.ag. Webhook routes at lines 9-10 use the same authMiddleware.
/v1/webhooks* branch (lines 40-53): token taken from URL query robotToken and compared with != to NILO_ROBOT_TOKEN; empty env returns 500.

/v1/events* branch (lines 55-67): the same env var is compared (non-constant-time) against the Authorization header after TrimPrefix 'Bearer robotToken='; a bare token also passes. No scoping by purpose.
After auth, service, consumer_id and expected_cursor are taken from the query string (lines 36-52) with no further authorization or allow-list; calls GrafanaResolver().UnblockConsumer.

Publishes a consumer-unblock UnblockMessage to Pub/Sub (line 165). The job handler in internal/cloud.go (lines 126-155) then calls unblock<Service>Consumer, which skips the event, and notifyEventSkipped posts to Slack.

evidence.description: Webhook credential read from URL query parameter robotToken.
Plain != comparison on the secret (not subtle.ConstantTimeCompare).
TrimPrefix on 'Bearer robotToken=' does not enforce the prefix; the same NILO_ROBOT_TOKEN value authorizes the unblock action.

CORS allows only https://obs.nile.ag. This is a browser-origin constraint, not an authentication control, and it confirms the endpoint is called from browser JavaScript (so the token is held in Grafana action config).

Sibling Slack routes (events/slack, commands/horus, webhooks/slack/actions) are not wrapped by authMiddleware; they presumably use their own Slack signature checks, which were not reviewed here and are out of scope for this candidate.

blockers: Who can read the Sentry/Grafana webhook URL, the Grafana action configuration (which holds the unblock bearer token), and Cloud Run request logs (which may record the query string) is not visible in source.

It is unknown whether Sentry/Grafana admins or log readers already hold equivalent operational authority to skip consumer events. If they do, this is same-principal authority and not a boundary violation.
Network exposure and ingress of the nilocloud Cloud Run service (public or restricted) is not in source.

validation_plan.local: Source-only: confirm in a unit test (owner-run, no network) that authMiddleware accepts a bare token on /v1/events/unblock and that no other check exists between the middleware and pubsub.SendMessage. Grep deployment manifests for where NILO_ROBOT_TOKEN is injected and whether the same secret is used for any other service.
validation_plan.deployment: Owner-observed, non-destructive: (1) list who has view access to the Sentry integration webhook URL and the Grafana contact point and table-action configuration; (2) check whether Cloud Run request logs for nilocloud record query strings and who has logging.viewer on that project; (3) check Cloud Run ingress and IAM for the service. Otherwise downgrade to hardening: use separate per-purpose tokens, move the webhook token into a header, and use subtle.ConstantTimeCompare.

title: nilocloud /v1/subscriptions/* routes have no effective authentication (discarded r.WithContext result); unauthenticated callers can drive Pub/Sub job dispatch
description: authMiddleware matches the /v1/subscriptions prefix but its only action is calling r.WithContext(...) and discarding the returned request. No token, secret, or OIDC/JWT check is performed. POST /v1/subscriptions/nilo is wrapped only by this middleware and passes caller-supplied base64 message data straight to handlePubSubMessage, which dispatches privileged ops jobs (nexport pipeline start/pause/export/import/resume, consumer-unblock cursor skipping across six services, mache store restore). POST /v1/subscriptions/cloudbuild is equally open and feeds Slack notification logic. The service is deployed with --allow-unauthenticated in cloudbuild.yaml. Sibling prefixes /v1/webhooks, /v1/events and /v1/mache each do enforce a token, so the missing check on /v1/subscriptions is an outlier. The downstream gRPC Jobs handlers (ledger/administrator ops Jobs) perform no user or role check, so the discarded robot identity is not a hidden control; nilocloud's own gRPC calls carry through, and the job runs regardless.
root_cause: The middleware branch for /v1/subscriptions does `r.WithContext(auth.NewContexWithUser(...UsrRobot()))` and drops the result (http.Request.WithContext returns a new request). Even if it had been used, it would only inject a robot identity into the context rather than verify the caller. No Pub/Sub push OIDC token verification exists anywhere in the nilocloud handler chain (handlers.go mux, main.go has only sentryhttp wrapping).
intended_behavior: Only Google Pub/Sub push (and Cloud Build via Pub/Sub) should be able to invoke these handlers: verify the Google-signed OIDC bearer token (issuer accounts.google.com, audience = service URL, email = the push subscription service account), or at minimum a shared secret like the sibling prefixes, and reject otherwise with 401.

title: Internal gRPC services trust caller identity from unauthenticated metadata; reachability depends on Cloud Run exposure
description: The shared gRPC server (thoth.Resolver.ServerGRPC) registers no transport credentials and no authentication interceptor, only jetgrpc and serverUnaryInterceptor. serverUnaryInterceptor builds the request user from the caller-supplied metadata key user-firebase-id. The reserved values Robot, RobotFreshMark, RobotInputs, RobotVilla and Unauthed map directly to in-memory users with no credential check. Robot users have PartyTypeAdmin, an AdminProfileID, and for Robot also RoleRobot. Any other value goes to the default branch. There, an optional user-auth-token is only tried via UserFromToken, and a failure is ignored. The code then falls back to ContextWithUser, which loads the user by ID from Firebase (authClient.UserByID) with no credential at all. So the fallback is reachable whenever the token is empty, invalid or mismatched, which means a caller who knows a Firebase UID can act as that user. Source shows no other auth layer: all six services (librarian, ledger, harvester, trader, postman, administrator) call ServerGRPC() and add nothing else in main.go. Their cloudbuild.yaml files deploy with --allow-unauthenticated and no ingress restriction flag. Whether an external attacker can actually reach these ports (Cloud Run ingress setting, any out-of-band IAM change, network path) cannot be established from source. I found no source control that blocks the claim. This is a deployment fact, so the finding stays needs_validation and is not confirmed.
claimed_root_cause: Service-to-service identity propagation uses plaintext gRPC metadata (user-firebase-id) that the server accepts as authoritative. Reserved robot IDs need no proof, and the Firebase-lookup fallback runs without verifying the token. Authentication therefore rests entirely on network or IAM isolation, which the deploy config does not enforce (--allow-unauthenticated).

trace.description: Reads user-firebase-id and user-auth-token from incoming gRPC metadata, which is attacker-controllable if the service port is reachable.
Reserved IDs (Unauthed, Robot, RobotFreshMark, RobotInputs, RobotVilla) are turned into robot or admin users without any credential check.
The token check is optional. If the token is empty, invalid or mismatched, the code falls through to ContextWithUser with the claimed ID.
Loads the user by claimed Firebase UID (authClient.UserByID) and installs it in the request context via auth.NewContexWithUser, so handlers authorize as that user.

evidence.description: ServerGRPC options contain no grpc.Creds and no auth interceptor; the chain is jetgrpc plus serverUnaryInterceptor only.
UsrRobot returns an admin-party user (AdminIDNile) with RoleRobot; the other robots (lines 207 to 242) are admin-party too.
Services use thothResolver.ServerGRPC() unmodified; the same call is in librarian:80, harvester:72, trader:63, postman:76 and administrator:70.
Cloud Run deploy uses --allow-unauthenticated with no ingress restriction flag; the same applies to the other services (librarian:40).
Clients dial with TLS when the host contains 443, which gives encryption but no caller authentication.

blockers: Cloud Run ingress setting (all, internal, internal-and-cloud-load-balancing) and any out-of-band IAM or invoker changes for each gRPC service are not in source.
Whether the service URLs are discoverable and reachable from the internet, and whether a front proxy or VPC controls sit in front of them, is not in source.
Source cannot show which handlers behind this interceptor expose sensitive operations, so impact depends on a service-by-service check.

validation_plan.deployment: The owner should run read-only gcloud queries: gcloud run services describe <svc> --region europe-west4 and check the ingress annotation (run.googleapis.com/ingress), then gcloud run services get-iam-policy <svc> and check whether allUsers holds roles/run.invoker. Use the same project that the deploy cloudbuild.yaml targets. Also check whether the service URLs appear in any public DNS or client config. Do not send live requests with forged metadata. If ingress is 'internal' or the invoker is restricted to the caller services' service accounts, downgrade or reject. If it is 'all' with allUsers invoker, upgrade to confirmed with high or critical severity, since robot admin identity gives cross-tenant access.
